Defining Macronutrients

The spec gives a precise definition that examiners expect you to reproduce: macronutrients are “a class of chemical compounds which humans consume in the largest quantities.” There are three: protein, fats (lipids), and carbohydrates. These are the nutrients you eat in gram-sized amounts every day — contrasted with micronutrients (vitamins, minerals), which are needed in milligram or microgram quantities. Getting this definition word-for-word correct is a reliable early mark on any principles of nutrition question.

Key Fact

Energy values to memorise: protein provides 4 kcal per gram; carbohydrate provides 4 kcal per gram; fat provides 9 kcal per gram. Fat is more than double the energy density of the other two macronutrients — relevant when planning diets for athletes (high energy needs) or those managing weight.

Protein: Essential and Non-Essential Amino Acids

Proteins are chains of amino acids. There are twenty amino acids in total, but the spec focuses on the split between essential and non-essential. Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from food. The nine on the spec are: histidine, isoleucine, lysine, leucine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. Non-essential amino acids — including alanine, asparagine, aspartic acid and glutamic acid — can be synthesised by the body from other compounds.

Foods that contain all nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts are called high biological-value (HBV) proteins. Animal foods — meat, fish, poultry, eggs, dairy — are HBV. Most plant proteins are low biological-value (LBV) because they lack one or more essential amino acids. Soya and quinoa are notable exceptions — both are complete plant proteins. For a 14-year-old vegan athlete, combining lentil curry with brown rice at dinner provides a complete amino acid profile, because lentils are low in methionine (plentiful in rice) and rice is low in lysine (plentiful in lentils).

The primary functions of protein are: growth and repair of body tissues; production of enzymes, hormones and antibodies; and as a secondary energy source (the body uses protein for energy when carbohydrate stores are depleted). Recommended daily intake for adults is approximately 0.75 g per kg of body weight — higher for adolescents, pregnant women and those recovering from illness or surgery.

Fats, Oils and Lipids

Dietary fats are classified by their chemical structure — specifically by the number of double bonds between carbon atoms in their fatty acid chains. Saturated fats have no double bonds and tend to be solid at room temperature. They are found mainly in animal products (butter, lard, fatty meat, full-fat dairy, palm oil) and are associated with raised LDL (“bad”) cholesterol and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) when consumed in excess. Monounsaturated fats have one double bond. Olive oil, rapeseed oil, avocados and most nuts are rich in monounsaturated fats; they are associated with a more favourable cholesterol profile.

Polyunsaturated fats have two or more double bonds. This category includes the essential fatty acids — omega-3 (alpha-linolenic acid) and omega-6 (linoleic acid) — which cannot be synthesised by the body and must be obtained from food. Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) are the richest source of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids, which support brain function, reduce inflammation, and lower triglyceride levels. Vegetable oils such as sunflower and corn oil are high in omega-6. The current dietary advice is to increase omega-3 intake and moderate omega-6, since Western diets tend to be omega-6 heavy.

The functions of dietary fat extend beyond energy: fat carries and enables absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; provides insulation for organs; and supplies essential fatty acids that the body cannot make. A diet very low in fat may therefore lead to deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins even if those vitamins are consumed — because without fat, they cannot be absorbed in the small intestine.

High intake of saturated fat → raised LDL cholesterol in the blood → LDL deposits on artery walls → formation of plaques (atherosclerosis) → narrowed arteries → increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) or stroke. The key vocabulary to use in an exam: saturated fat, LDL cholesterol, atherosclerosis, coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease. A student who writes “saturated fat causes heart disease” scores 1 mark; a student who writes the full chain using this vocabulary scores much more in an extended response.

Carbohydrates: Monosaccharides, Disaccharides and Polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred energy source. They are classified by the number of sugar units they contain. Monosaccharides are single sugar units: glucose (found in fruit and honey; the form of sugar the body uses for energy), fructose (fruit sugar) and galactose (found in milk). Disaccharides are two monosaccharides bonded together: sucrose (glucose + fructose — table sugar), lactose (glucose + galactose — milk sugar), and maltose (glucose + glucose — from malt). Polysaccharides are long chains of glucose units. Starch (from plants: potatoes, flour, rice) and glycogen (stored in the liver and muscle) are digestible polysaccharides. Non-starch polysaccharides (NSP) — dietary fibre — are not digested in the small intestine, passing instead to the colon where they feed beneficial bacteria and support bowel health.

Starchy polysaccharides release energy more slowly than simple sugars because they require digestion before glucose enters the bloodstream. This is why a bowl of porridge oats before a 5 km run sustains energy better than a spoonful of sugar — the polysaccharide structure means glucose is absorbed gradually, maintaining a stable blood sugar level rather than a rapid spike and crash. This is particularly important for managing type 2 diabetes, where the glycaemic response to food is a key dietary concern.

Key Fact

Monosaccharides: glucose, fructose, galactose. Disaccharides: sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), maltose. Polysaccharides: starch, glycogen, non-starch polysaccharides (dietary fibre). The written paper can ask students to classify a named carbohydrate — knowing which group each falls into is a reliable recall mark.

Malnutrition means ‘wrong nutrition’ in either direction — too much or too little. Protein deficiency causes stunted growth, poor wound healing, muscle wasting and impaired immunity; in severe global poverty, the condition kwashiorkor (characterised by oedema) can develop. Excess protein puts strain on the kidneys, which must excrete the nitrogenous waste. Excess saturated fat raises CVD risk and contributes to obesity; fat deficiency impairs fat-soluble vitamin absorption and disrupts hormone production. Excess refined carbohydrate / free sugars contributes to type 2 diabetes, dental caries and obesity; insufficient carbohydrate causes fatigue and forces the body to break down protein and fat for energy, producing ketones. For the exam, tie each consequence to a named individual (e.g. an obese adult, a vegan with inadequate protein, a child with dental caries) to access AO2 application marks.

What Does ‘Developing a Recipe’ Actually Mean?

Developing a recipe is more than swapping one ingredient for another. The spec is explicit that food development requires decisions about four things together: ingredients, processes, cooking methods and portion sizes. A student who answers “replace butter with low-fat spread” and stops there has changed only one ingredient — that is an incomplete adaptation. A thorough response considers all four levers: for example, replacing butter with olive oil (ingredient), switching from creaming to folding (process), changing from shallow-frying to grilling (cooking method), and reducing the serving portion to manage overall calorie intake (portion size).

This lesson brings together everything from the rest of the unit — nutrition knowledge, food science, dietary needs, sensory evaluation — and applies it to a practical brief. In your exam, extended-response questions at 8 or 12 marks often present a named person with a specific need and ask you to evaluate how well a set of adaptations would meet that need. The ability to justify and explain your choices, and to weigh strengths and weaknesses against each other, is what separates top-band answers from mid-band ones.

Key Fact

The four levers of recipe development are: ingredients (what goes in), processes (how ingredients are prepared and combined), cooking methods (how heat is applied), and portion sizes (how much is served). Exam answers that change only the ingredients are incomplete — always consider all four.

Adapting Recipes for Dietary Needs

The spec requires students to plan and adapt recipes for a range of specific dietary needs. The most commonly tested examples are:

Coeliac disease. People with coeliac disease have an autoimmune reaction to gluten, the protein in wheat, barley and rye. Even a small amount can damage the lining of the small intestine and impair nutrient absorption. Adapting a recipe for a coeliac person requires replacing all gluten-containing flour with alternatives such as rice flour, buckwheat flour or certified gluten-free oat flour. However, this is a process change too: gluten provides the stretchy network that traps gas and gives baked goods their structure. Gluten-free baking often needs xanthan gum (a stabiliser) or an extra egg to replicate this structural function, or the resulting cake will be crumbly and dense.

Type 2 diabetes. People with type 2 diabetes need to manage blood glucose levels by reducing free sugars and increasing dietary fibre (NSP), which slows glucose absorption. Recipe adaptation might include: replacing white flour with wholemeal (ingredient), using smaller portions of starchy foods (portion size), choosing steaming over roasting with oil (cooking method) to reduce the overall energy density, and using naturally sweet vegetables like butternut squash to reduce added sugar (ingredient). The aim is a lower glycaemic load overall, not just one ingredient swap.

Lactose intolerance. People who cannot digest lactose (the sugar in milk) need recipes that replace dairy milk, butter and cream with lactose-free alternatives: plant-based milks (oat, almond, soya), dairy-free spread or coconut cream. The sensory properties of the dish may change: oat milk has a sweeter flavour than cows’ milk; coconut cream adds richness but also a coconut aroma that may not be appropriate for a savoury dish.

Vegetarian and vegan diets. The spec distinguishes three vegetarian categories. Lacto-ovo vegetarians eat dairy and eggs but not meat or fish. Lacto vegetarians eat dairy but not eggs or meat. Vegans exclude all animal products. Adapting a beef lasagne for a lacto-ovo vegetarian requires replacing minced beef with a protein alternative such as Quorn, lentils or a combination — but the rest of the sauce and béchamel can remain unchanged. Adapting the same dish for a vegan requires also replacing the dairy milk in the béchamel and the Parmesan cheese on top. A key nutritional consideration for vegans is ensuring adequate vitamin B12, iron and calcium, which are less bioavailable from plant sources than animal sources.

A very common marking pitfall is to name one ingredient substitution and present it as a complete recipe adaptation. The spec and mark schemes expect students to consider all four levers (ingredients, processes, cooking methods, portion sizes). In a 12-mark Evaluate question about adapting a dish for a named individual, a top-band response will typically change at least two levers and explain why each change addresses the brief, what sensory or functional consequence that change has, and whether the benefit outweighs any drawback. For example: “Replacing plain white flour with wholemeal in the pastry case increases fibre content (ingredient), but wholemeal flour contains less gluten-forming protein, meaning the pastry will be crumblier and harder to roll thin (consequence). To compensate, a small amount of plain flour could be retained in a 50/50 blend (further adaptation), which preserves some workability while still increasing the NSP content compared to the original recipe (justified judgement).”

Managing Time, Cost and Lifestyle

Recipe development does not happen in isolation from real-world constraints. The spec specifically mentions working parents needing dishes that are quick to prepare and cook. When developing a recipe for this group, time management is a design criterion alongside nutrition. Techniques that save time include: batch cooking (making a large quantity and freezing in portions); preparing ingredients in advance (a mirepoix of onion, carrot and celery can be refrigerated for 3 days); choosing cooking methods with shorter active cooking time (a stir-fry takes 8 minutes from wok to plate; a slow stew needs 2 hours even if most of that is unattended).

Cost is a parallel constraint. A low-budget recipe adaptation might replace chicken breast (higher cost per kg) with chicken thighs (lower cost, more fat but more flavour), or substitute fresh herbs with dried to reduce waste. Per-portion costing — dividing the total ingredient cost by the number of servings — is a practical skill the spec expects students to use when justifying recipe decisions.

Testing, Evaluating and Improving Recipes

Once a recipe adaptation has been tried, it must be evaluated against the original brief. The process mirrors sensory evaluation (covered in Lesson 6): the adapted dish is tasted and assessed for appearance, aroma, flavour, texture and — where relevant — sound. Sensory descriptors should be precise: not “it tasted nice” but “the wholemeal pastry had a nutty, slightly bitter flavour and a coarser texture compared to the original.”

Adjusting seasoning is explicitly mentioned in the spec as part of the development cycle. Salt enhances and balances other flavours — a dish that tastes flat may need salt rather than more of another ingredient. Acid (lemon juice, vinegar) brightens flavour; sugar balances acidity. Learning to identify which flavour dimension is missing and adjusting accordingly is a core practical skill.

After testing, the developer produces a justified evaluation: a clear explanation of what changes were made, why they were made, how they meet the nutritional or lifestyle brief, and what further improvements could be made. In an exam question, “justify” means provide reasons that weigh the benefit of the change against any potential drawback.

The spec gives steaming instead of boiling as its example of choosing an appropriate technique for a specific outcome. This is worth remembering as a model for how the principle works. When broccoli is boiled, water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C, B vitamins) leach into the cooking water; if that water is discarded, up to 50% of the vitamin C can be lost. When the same broccoli is steamed, it is never submerged in water, so much less vitamin loss occurs — the sensory outcome (colour, slight bite) is also generally preferred. The same principle applies to other cooking-method swaps: grilling rather than shallow-frying reduces fat content; baking rather than deep-frying a potato changes the texture (soft interior but without added fat from frying). Every method swap must be justified by explaining what the benefit is and whether any sensory or structural trade-off results.

Key Fact

Choosing the right technique is part of recipe development. Steaming instead of boiling preserves water-soluble vitamins because the food is not submerged. Grilling instead of frying reduces total fat. Wholemeal instead of white flour increases NSP but can make pastry crumblier. For every technique swap in a development answer, state the benefit AND any sensory or structural consequence.

What Is Cuisine?

The word “cuisine” is often used loosely to mean “food from a country” — but the spec gives a precise definition that examiners use in mark schemes. Cuisine is a style characteristic of a particular country or region, where it has developed historically through three pillars: (1) distinctive ingredients; (2) specific preparation and cooking methods or equipment; and (3) presentation and serving techniques. Top-band answers cite all three pillars, not just a list of dishes.

All cuisines have evolved over time, shaped by climate (which determines which crops grow locally), trade routes (which introduced new spices, grains and cooking fats), migration and cultural exchange, and more recently by industrialisation, food technology and globalisation. What we call “traditional” cuisine in any country is itself the product of centuries of change — tomatoes did not arrive in Italy until the 16th century, yet are now central to Italian cooking; chillies are fundamental to Indian and Mexican cookery but were unknown in those regions before the 16th century.

British Cuisine

British cuisine draws on a long history of farming, fishing and trading, as well as significant cultural influences from centuries of migration and empire. It is characterised by a reliance on seasonal, locally produced ingredients: root vegetables (parsnips, carrots, turnips), brassicas (cabbage, Brussels sprouts, kale), dairy (butter, cream, cheddar cheese), lamb, beef and pork, and freshwater and sea fish (cod, haddock, mackerel, salmon, trout).

Traditional British cooking methods reflect the country’s cold, wet climate and a preference for substantial, warming food. Roasting (a Sunday roast with roast beef or lamb, roast potatoes and seasonal vegetables), braising (a lamb shank braised slowly in stock), stewing (a beef and stout stew, a Lancashire hotpot), baking (a Victoria sandwich, shortcrust pastry pies, scones) and grilling (grilled kippers, a full English breakfast) are all central techniques. Many British dishes are one-pot or slow-cooked — designed to make the most of cheaper cuts of meat that become tender through long, moist cooking.

Regional British cuisines reflect local ingredients and history. Scottish cuisine features oatmeal (porridge, haggis, oatcakes), salmon, venison and raspberries. Welsh cuisine celebrates cawl (a lamb and leek broth), Welsh rarebit (a cooked cheese sauce on toast), and lamb from upland farms. Northern English cuisine is famous for Yorkshire pudding, pork pies, Lancashire hotpot and Eccles cakes. West Country cooking in England features clotted cream, Cheddar cheese, cider-braised meats and freshly caught fish. The presentation style of traditional British food is typically hearty and unfussy — a plate laid out with portions of meat, potatoes and vegetables, rather than elaborate plating.

Modern Variations in British Cooking

Contemporary British cooking has been transformed by multicultural influences, changing nutritional guidelines, and new cooking equipment. A home kitchen in 2025 is just as likely to produce a chicken tikka masala (now regarded by many as a British dish through the British South Asian community’s contribution to food culture) as a toad-in-the-hole. New equipment — slow cookers, air fryers, steamers, immersion blenders — has changed cooking methods. Nutritional awareness has encouraged chefs and home cooks to reduce saturated fat (choosing lean cuts, steaming instead of deep-frying), reduce salt and increase vegetables and whole grains. A modern Victoria sandwich might use a lower-sugar filling or a wholemeal flour proportion that would have been unusual a generation ago.

Key Fact

Cuisine is defined by THREE pillars: (1) distinctive ingredients, (2) specific preparation and cooking methods or equipment, (3) presentation and serving techniques. When writing about any cuisine in your exam, structure your answer around all three pillars — a list of dishes alone does not reach the top band.

Italian Cuisine

Italian cuisine is one of the most recognised and widely influential in the world, characterised by its emphasis on high-quality, simply prepared ingredients. Regional variation is strong: the north (Piedmont, Lombardy) relies on butter, cream, rice (risotto) and polenta; the south (Campania, Sicily) favours olive oil, tomatoes, fresh vegetables, seafood and dried pasta.

Distinctive ingredients: durum wheat pasta (spaghetti, penne, tagliatelle, rigatoni), short-grain Arborio rice (risotto), semolina (gnocchi), San Marzano tomatoes, extra-virgin olive oil, Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese, mozzarella, prosciutto, basil, garlic and seasonal vegetables. Bread (ciabatta, focaccia) plays a central role, and the Italian approach is to use a few excellent-quality ingredients rather than many.

Preparation and cooking methods: making fresh pasta by hand (mixing semolina or ‘00’ flour with eggs, kneading and rolling by hand or with a pasta machine); slow braising (ossà buccà — braised veal shin in white wine and gremolata); slow simmering of ragù sauces for several hours; wood-fired pizza baking at very high temperatures (400–500°C); the risotto technique of gradual stock absorption with constant stirring to achieve a creamy starch-release from the Arborio grain. Risotto technique is a direct application of gelatinisation in practice — the starch granules in the rice absorb liquid and swell as they are stirred.

Presentation and meal structure: a traditional Italian meal follows a multi-course structure: antipasto (starter, often cured meats, olives, bruschetta), primo (first course — pasta, risotto or soup), secondo (main course — meat or fish) with a separate contorno (side dish of vegetables), then dolce (dessert) and coffee. This structure separates carbohydrate and protein courses in a way that is quite different from the British single-plate model.

Japanese Cuisine

Japanese cuisine has developed over two millennia in an island nation with a long coastline, mountainous terrain and four distinct seasons. The result is a cuisine defined by seasonality, restraint, precision and respect for natural flavours — the philosophy of shun (eating food at the peak of its season) underpins Japanese cooking at every level.

Distinctive ingredients: Japanese short-grain rice (the staple of nearly every meal, from plain steamed rice to sushi rice seasoned with rice vinegar, sugar and salt); dashi (a light stock made from kombu seaweed and dried bonito flakes, which provides the savoury umami flavour base for miso soup and many sauces); soy sauce; miso paste; tofu; nori (dried seaweed); mirin (sweet rice wine for cooking); sake; fresh fish and shellfish (particularly salmon, tuna, sea bream, mackerel and prawns); and a wide range of pickled vegetables. Japanese cuisine features very little dairy and traditionally very little red meat.

Preparation and cooking methods: precision cutting is fundamental — sashimi requires very thin, even slices of raw fish made with a single-draw stroke of a specialist knife; katsuramuki involves peeling a vegetable such as daikon radish into a single continuous paper-thin sheet. Steaming is common (steamed rice, steamed dumplings). Grilling over charcoal (yakitori skewered chicken; teriyaki glazed fish or meat). Tempura — vegetables or seafood dipped in a very light, cold batter and flash-fried at high temperature — uses a technique specifically designed to produce a delicate, barely-there coating rather than a thick crust. Fermentation features strongly: miso, soy sauce and sake are all fermented products.

Presentation and meal structure: Japanese presentation emphasises visual harmony, balance and seasonality. A traditional Japanese meal (ichijuu sansai — “one soup three sides”) is served simultaneously in small bowls and plates: a bowl of steamed rice, a bowl of miso soup, and three small side dishes of protein and vegetables. Colours, textures and the shapes of the dishes complement each other. The meal structure is not sequential (as in France or Italy) but simultaneous. Portion sizes are modest and the emphasis is on variety rather than volume.

All cuisines continue to evolve. In Italy, traditional hand-rolled pasta made with a mattarello (rolling pin) on a wooden board has largely been replaced in home kitchens by the pasta machine or even bought dried pasta; the ragù that once simmered for six hours can be approximated in an electric pressure cooker in 45 minutes. In Japan, western influences since the Meiji era (1868) introduced beef, pork, bread and dairy — giving rise to distinctly Japanese-western hybrid dishes such as katsu (deep-fried breaded pork or chicken, served with rice and a tangy Worcestershire-based sauce). In Britain, the slow cooker has revived braised and stewed dishes that require little active cooking time. Modern dietary guidelines have driven reformulation: lower salt in soups and stocks, less butter in pastry, more wholegrain in bread. These adaptations change the use of food commodities without abandoning the fundamental character of the cuisine.

A persistent misconception is that “fusion cuisine” — dishes that deliberately blend culinary traditions from different cultures — is somehow less authentic than a cuisine tied to a single nation or region. In reality, no cuisine has ever been static. Tomatoes and chillies, now central to Italian and Indian cooking respectively, arrived in those countries only in the 16th century via the Americas. Japanese katsu (deep-fried breaded pork) is a deliberate Meiji-era fusion of European schnitzel technique with Japanese rice and sauce. Authenticity in cuisine is better understood as internal consistency — using a cuisine’s techniques, flavour principles and meal structure — rather than purity of ingredient origin. For your exam, this matters when comparing traditional versus modern variations: a modern British curry can be both “British” and an expression of authentic South Asian culinary tradition.

Key Fact

Meal structures differ dramatically across cultures: Italy’s sequential multi-course structure (antipasto → primo → secondo → dolce); Japan’s simultaneous one-soup-three-sides model; Britain’s single-plate format. These structural differences reflect cultural values around eating (communal pacing, visual harmony, hearty efficiency) as much as the ingredients or cooking methods.
